it: You began your career at MoMA in 1973 and founded their video-media exhibition and collection programs in 1974 with video art still in its infancy. What gave you the confidence and clarity to believe that this hyper-contemporary work would remain relevant—not only for years and decades, but we can now safely say, for good?
You began your career at MoMA in 1973 and founde
What made you sure in 1974 that video art would last?
You mentioned how you were able to find these early gems. Can you talk more about how you were able to get access to artists, like Nam June Paik, in the early days?
You mentioned how you were able to find these ea
How did you first reach artists like Nam June Paik?

Your experience really highlights the centrality of curiosity. When you were talking about institutionalizing the form, you mentioned needing to reach out for internal support to legitimize what you were doing, perhaps from trustees like Mrs. John D. Rockefeller III. But did you also get any pushback for the medium being so new? Was there a sense that video work didn't belong in MoMA next to a Picasso?
Your experience really highlights the centrality
Did video seem out of place in MoMA next to a Picasso?

In addition to how connected you were to the New York scene, you seemed to know what was going on everywhere. I’m wondering about another pocket forming around this time but in Chicago, with its burgeoning computer video art scene in particular at the University of Illinois at Chicago. That's where Tom DeFanti and Dan Sandin founded the Electronic Visualization Lab [EVL] in 1973. They developed the Sandin Image Processor—which artists like Cory Arcangel still use to this day — and GRASS, one of the earliest computer animation programs. You knew about the work and even included it in MoMA’s sem
In addition to how connected you were to the New
How did you get to know Chicago’s experimental video scene?

How did artists working with computer video, like Lillian Schwartz, come across your radar? I'm wondering if you have any insight as to why single-channel videotape seemed to gain institutional acceptance more easily than this early computer video art. You were drawn to both. You even showed Lillian's work at the end of 1975 in a show called Computer Video .
How did artists working with computer video, lik
Why did single-channel videotape win institutional acceptance faster than computer video like Lillian Schwartz’s?

Even in 1968 Lillian was one of the E.A.T. competition winners in MoMA's The Machine as Seen at the End of the Mechanical Age . That time at the end of the ‘60s seemed to be when interest in computer and digital art peaked. When you arrived by the early-mid '70s, it appeared that institutional interest had largely disappeared—like you said for a variety of reasons. It was mostly dismissed and took several more decades to be reassessed.
Even in 1968 Lillian was one of the E.A.T. compe
Was computer art largely dismissed by institutions after its late 1960s peak?

It’s an impossible task. People collecting and studying all the contemporary work today—with hindsight from 40, 50 years—will surely overlook and miss things. Someone who worked with and was greatly inspired by the Whitney brothers was Larry Cuba. I bring him up because he was particularly interested in sound, like you. As the ‘80s wore on, what did you think about the work of experimental digital filmmakers like Cuba?
It’s an impossible task. People collecting and s
What did you think of experimental digital filmmakers like Larry Cuba in the 1980s?

It seems like today, including sound with moving visuals can feel old-fashioned. But in a lot of ways that sound work of Paik, Viola, Cuba—even going back earlier to Oskar Fischinger—and the Whitney brothers is still so impressive. It seems like something that’s been a bit lost today. Having said that, your podcast, Barbara London Calling , does an outstanding job of highlighting artists who do emphasize sound and visuals in a multidisciplinary way, like Ryoji Ikeda.
It seems like today, including sound with moving
How does your podcast, Barbara London Calling, spotlight sound-and-image artists like Ryoji Ikeda?

Incredible. You mentioned how with experimental film, the greater world didn’t really know what to do with it. Now in 2025, we have emerging technologies in art, like blockchain and AI. They're also largely met with skepticism from the outside world—similar to computer art in the '70s. Do you see a connection and how do you view contemporary artists like Auriea Harvey, Kim Asendorf, Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst, who engage with these emerging tools today?
Incredible. You mentioned how with experimental
Do blockchain and AI artists like Auriea Harvey face the skepticism computer art met?

Certainly. She’s had a decades-long practice as one of the original net artists. Why do you think that net art was accepted more quickly, whereas most of these other emerging technologies in art we’ve mentioned face more skepticism? It seems to be the exception to the rule.
Certainly. She’s had a decades-long practice as
Why was net art, like Auriea Harvey’s, accepted faster than other new media?

I’m fascinated by how museums balance what is happening now with their long-term time horizons and perspectives. What do you see as some of the most significant moments in bringing video art to prominence within the museum context? What were its breakthrough moments?
I’m fascinated by how museums balance what is ha
What were the breakthrough moments that brought video art to prominence in museums?
These are milestones in new media art history. Around the time of your 1985 Music Video show, were you aware of Rebecca Allen and her computer music videos she was making with Kraftwerk ?
These are milestones in new media art history. A
Did you know Rebecca Allen’s Kraftwerk videos during your 1985 Music Video show?

These next few questions focus more on your curatorial perspective—more about giving advice. We want to learn from such a unique and celebrated career as yours. In your observation, what is missing in the curatorial landscape of time-based media shows today?
These next few questions focus more on your cura
What is missing from the curatorial landscape of time-based media shows today?

That’s great advice. Community seems to be playing an expanding role these days. You've organized so many shows throughout your career and at a major institution like MoMA. What are some of the most important considerations at the installation level—when you're thinking about installing a show in a physical space—for time-based media shows?
That’s great advice. Community seems to be playi
What matters most when installing time-based media shows in a physical space?
Tapping into the expertise of others and honest dialogue with the artists seem to be key. How do you begin the process for a thematic or group exhibition? Do you start with an idea, funding, artists?
Tapping into the expertise of others and honest
Does a group show start with an idea, funding or artists?

Today, when you keep your ears and eyes open, you’re inundated with a seemingly overwhelming amount of information. How were you—and are you—able to sift through what's important in the moment, especially thinking about work to acquire?
Today, when you keep your ears and eyes open, yo
How do you sift what matters from today’s flood of information, especially for acquisitions?
A focus of ours this year at Le Random is preserving digital culture. How do you navigate between allowing work to evolve over time versus maintaining its original aesthetic?
A focus of ours this year at Le Random is preser
In preservation, how do you balance a work’s evolution against its original look?
